claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline passivating surface layer or by a particle-refined microstructure containing phases such as TiB2.
An ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer can produce low friction and high wear resistance in CoCrFeMnNi.
The dynamically refined surface enhances passive-film stability during corrosive sliding.
A dynamically refined or boron-doped HEA has lower wear and corrosion rates than a conventional coarse-grained HEA.
The proposed initial alloys are homogeneous and relatively coarse grained, without a preexisting ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer.
Boron addition to an AlCoCrFeNiMoTi-based coating promotes in situ formation of TiB2 and refinement of the BCC phase.
Sliding or abrasive deformation in a corrosive environment triggers dynamic surface grain refinement.
Mechanical and corrosive loading favors redistribution or precipitation of microalloying-induced particles at the surface.
Inverse Hall-Petch behavior in an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer lowers shear strength and friction.
A refined surface permits development of a more stable, defect-minimized passive film.
The treated alloy will exhibit lower wear volume, wear rate, and friction coefficient than the matched baseline.
The treated alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion current density than the matched baseline during the proposed comparison.
Combined degradation will be lower than the sum of independently measured wear and corrosion contributions.
The baseline has a coarse-grained microstructure and a less stable passive film under the same conditions.
The predicted benefit holds at loads that induce adequate but nonexcessive deformation and permit a stable nanocrystalline layer to form.
Excessive load can cause catastrophic spallation and eliminate the predicted benefit.
Oversized secondary particles can become spall-prone and introduce defects into the passive film.
A controlled test can compare a coarse-grained control and an engineered treatment under identical sliding conditions in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both wear rate and corrosion current density would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Dynamic nanocrystallization is described as being induced by sliding deformation, yet both groups receive identical sliding exposure while the baseline is defined as lacking induced dynamic nanocrystallization. No independent treatment is specified that ensures only the treatment group can develop the layer.

The hypothesis combines two materially distinct interventions—wear-induced nanocrystallization in CoCrFeMnNi and boron-induced TiB2 formation in an AlCoCrFeNiMoTi coating—as alternatives within one treatment, so the proposed comparison does not isolate a single mediator or mechanism.
